newsitem.title: USA: Kevorkian to offer mood music to go with his art.
newsitem.headline: Kevorkian to offer mood music to go with his art.

text.p: Assisted-suicide activist Jack Kevorkian, who literally put his sweat and blood into his second major art showing on Saturday, will offer some mood music to go with his growing collection of oil paintings.

A Los Angeles-based independent jazz recording label is planning to release a compact disc of Kevorkian's own compositions entitled "A Very Still Life: The Kevorkian Suite." The 68-year-old retired pathologist plays the flute on each track.

Chad Williams, owner of Resist Records, described the music as "sub jazz," a mixture of acid jazz and traditional bop. It will be released on the Lucid label in May in the United States, Japan and Italy and $4 of the $18.98 retail price will be donated to Kevorkian's efforts to open an assisted suicide clinic.
The disc's cover will feature his painting, "A Very Still Life," which shows a glowing iris growing out of a human skull sitting on a crimson cloth.
The painting is one of 13 on display at the Arianna Gallery, which include five new works in addition to eight paintings he displayed three years ago.

New works include "From Deir-ez-Zoir to Auschwitz: Genocide," which depicts a severed head being held by the hair by an Ottoman Turk soldier and a Nazi SS officer. The wooden frame has barbed wire nailed to it and is smeared with Kevorkian's own blood.

The retired pathologist, the son of Armenian immigrants, told reporters he wanted to draw comparisons between Turkish atrocities against Armenians in 1915 and the Jewish Holocaust during World War Two. The Armenian tragedy decimated his own family.
"It's as bad a holocaust as the Jewish holocaust, proportionately, and it should not be forgotten. But then, of course, I'm biased," Kevorkian said.

Kevorkian is not selling his original works, but the gallery is selling posters and computer-generated prints to help raise money for his cause. Ironically, he said he does not actually enjoy painting -- "because it's work" -- but does it to convey his ideas.
"I consider myself a cartoonist in oil," he said.

Also new is a portrait of composer Johann Sebastian Bach, who Kevorkian reveres as his personal idol and musical inspiration. Some of his Bach-style works have been transformed into jazz pieces for the forthcoming record.

Record label owner Williams insisted he was not merely cashing in on Kevorkian's novelty. "I don't think you can get past the novelty aspect of it, but the bottom line is this is going to be a good record and that's what's going to carry it.

Kevorkian, who will face trial on assisted suicide charges this summer in the small western Michigan town of Ionia, declined to say whether he had any involvement in three recent suicides, including that of a person dropped off at a coroner's office in his Volkswagen van.
He has acknowledged being present at 45 assisted suicides since his right-to-die crusade began in 1990.
